CausalChain: COL1A2 upregulation -> Increased collagen deposition -> ECM remodeling -> Activation of integrin/FAK/PI3K mechanotransduction -> Altered nuclear architecture and signaling -> Dysregulation of mRNA export factors (NUP62, NXF1) -> Aberrant mRNA export -> Enhanced metastasis/angiogenesis -> Poor liver cancer prognosis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in liver neoplasms, the overexpression of COL1A2 initiates a multistep process where enhanced collagen synthesis and ECM remodeling lead to increased ECM stiffness. This modified microenvironment activates cell-surface integrins and downstream FAK/PI3K/ROCK signaling pathways, which transmit mechanical and biochemical cues to the nucleus. These signals alter the organization and function of the nuclear pore complex, specifically downregulating or functionally impairing mRNA export factors such as NUP62 and NXF1. As a consequence, the export of key mRNAs involved in cell cycle regulation and apoptosis is disrupted, resulting in sustained activation of metastasis and angiogenesis-promoting pathways, thereby driving a more aggressive tumor phenotype and poorer clinical outcomes. This revised hypothesis integrates original elements concerning COL1A2-induced ECM remodeling and its downstream impact on mRNA export, while explicitly incorporating a mechanotransduction intermediary to account for the transition between extracellular alterations and nuclear dysfunction.
Abstract: We propose that in hepatocellular carcinoma, overexpression of COL1A2 promotes not only the accrual of collagen and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling but also initiates a mechanotransduction cascade that alters nuclear architecture, leading to dysregulation of mRNA export factors such as NUP62 and NXF1. Specifically, increased collagen deposition enhances ECM stiffness and activates integrin-mediated signaling pathways (e.g., FAK/PI3K/ROCK), which in turn modulate nuclear pore dynamics and gene regulatory networks. This cascade results in aberrant mRNA export, ultimately sustaining the pro-metastatic and angiogenic signaling responsible for aggressive cancer phenotypes and poor liver cancer prognosis. Our approach leverages advanced live-cell imaging, mechanobiology platforms, and single-cell transcriptomics to elucidate and validate this novel link between ECM remodeling and nuclear mRNA processing.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited a direct link between COL1A2-driven ECM remodeling and dysregulation of mRNA export without detailing the signaling intermediates. The revised hypothesis retains the original causal chain—COL1A2 overexpression leading to ECM alterations and subsequent mRNA export defects—but enhances it by incorporating a mechanotransduction pathway mediated by integrin/FAK/PI3K signaling. This addition provides a clear mechanistic bridge between ECM remodeling and nuclear function alterations, improves logical coherence, and suggests practical experimental approaches using contemporary technologies like live-cell imaging and single-cell transcriptomics to test the hypothesis.
